diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let Assumption \ref{assu:34} be satisfied. Then, for all~$p \in \N$ and~$\rho \in \R$, the family of matrices~$\{\K_n^p(\rho)\}_n$ defined in~\eqref{eq:21} is weakly well-conditioned.
For all $p \in \mathbb{N}$ with~$p \geq 1$, $h > 0$, and $\mu \in \R$, the variational formulation~\eqref{eq:10} admits a unique solution.
For~$p>1$, the larger support of B-splines does not provide sufficient insight to establish the invertibility of the system matrix through a linear algebra argument.
The method is proven to be unconditionally stable and preserves both mass and energy invariants at the final time.

issues.failure_explanation: The abstract and conclusions claim the method is (proven) unconditionally stable. What the paper actually establishes is Theorem 3.13, whose stability conclusion is conditional on Assumption 3.4 (unique solvability of the discrete problem for all p, h, mu), which the paper itself states it cannot verify for p>1 (only p=1 is justified). Hence unconditional stability is not proven for the maximal-regularity case p>=2 that the method targets, and the Conclusions' phrase 'proven to be unconditionally stable' misstates what is established.

failure_location.quote: We investigate the stability and conservation properties of the method, demonstrating that it preserves both mass and energy at the final time, and it is unconditionally stable.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Qualify the abstract/intro/conclusion statements: stability is proven under Assumption 3.4, which is verified only for p=1.
issues.overall_effect: The title-level, abstract, novelties and conclusions claims overstate the established guarantee; a reader may believe stability is unconditional, whereas it hinges on an assumption declared open for p>1.
issues.title: Abstract and conclusions assert unconditional stability without the unproven uniqueness assumption
issues.why_classification: Purely editorial qualification of summary prose; every formal result stands as stated and no mathematical content is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \mi \dpt \psi(t) + \mu \psi(t) = f(t) & t \in (0,T),
solves~\eqref{eq:9}, and due to the regularity assumption on~$f$, it is also a solution to~\eqref{eq:12}.
\mi (\dpt \psi, w)_{J_T} + \mu (\psi, w)_{J_T} = (f, w)_{J_T} \quad \text{for all~} w \in L^2(0,T).

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed function does not solve the IVP (9). Substituting psi = e^{-i*mu*t}(psi_0 + int_0^t e^{i*mu*s} f(s) ds) gives psi' = -i*mu*psi + f, hence i*psi' + mu*psi = 2*mu*psi + i*f, which equals f only in trivial cases (e.g. for f=0, psi_0=1, mu=1 it gives 2*e^{-it}, not 0). The correct solution of i*psi' + mu*psi = f, psi(0)=psi_0 is psi(t) = e^{i*mu*t} psi_0 - i*e^{i*mu*t} int_0^t e^{-i*mu*s} f(s) ds (the homogeneous solution is e^{+i*mu*t}, consistent with the eigen-expansion where mu can be negative). The existence claim of Proposition 3.2 is thus supported by a false computation, requiring multiple sign and factor corrections rather than a single forced fix.

failure_location.quote: \psi(t) = e^{-\mi \mu t} \psi_0 + e^{-\mi \mu t} \int_0^t e^{\mi \mu s} f(s) \dd s

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the displayed formula with the correct solution of (9).
issues.overall_effect: Only the existence part of the proof of Proposition 3.2 is affected; the proposition's claim remains true with the corrected formula, and no later result formally depends on this step.
issues.title: Wrong explicit solution formula in the existence step of Proposition 3.2
issues.why_classification: Local correction of a standard ODE solution formula; the statement of Proposition 3.2 and all downstream content survive unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: (\dpt \psi, e^{-\bullet/T} \dpt \psi)_{J_T} = \int_0^T \partial_s \psi(s) \partial_s \overline{\psi}(s) e^{-s/T} \dd s
We test~\eqref{eq:13} with~$w(t) = e^{-t/T} \dpt \psi(t)$.

issues.failure_explanation: By (14), the pairing (d/dt psi, w) with w = e^{-t/T} d/dt psi is the real nonnegative number int |psi'|^2 e^{-s/T} ds, so Re(i (d/dt psi, w)) = 0, not int |psi'|^2 e^{-s/T} ds. The correct real-part identity is 0 = mu*[(1/2T) int |psi|^2 e^{-s/T} + (1/2e)|psi(T)|^2], from which psi = 0 follows only for mu != 0 (mu = 0 needs the imaginary part). Moreover, even taking the printed identity at face value, the conclusion psi = 0 does not follow for mu < 0, since the first term is nonnegative and the mu-terms nonpositive and could cancel. The uniqueness claim (for all real mu) is thus unproved as written, although it is true via a corrected argument.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Recompute the real part (giving 0 = mu*[...]) and conclude for mu != 0; handle mu = 0 via the imaginary part, which yields int |psi'|^2 e^{-s/T} = 0.
issues.overall_effect: The uniqueness argument of Proposition 3.2 fails as written for mu < 0 (and for the printed computation, for all mu); the claim itself is salvageable, and Proposition 3.2 plays only a motivational role for the discrete analysis.
issues.title: Mis-evaluated real part invalidates the uniqueness argument in Proposition 3.2
issues.why_classification: Short local recomputation plus a routine sign case split; the proposition's statement and its role in the paper survive unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \B^p_h[\ell,j] := (\dpt \phi_j^p, \dpt \phi^p_{\ell-1})_{J_T}, \quad \bC^p_h[\ell,j] := (\dpt \phi_j^p, \phi^p_{\ell-1})_{J_T}
\mathbf{K}_h^p(\mu) := \mi \B_h^p - \mu \bC_h^p.
The matrices $\B_h^1$ and $\bC_h^1$ are lower triangular Toeplitz band matrices with three nonzero diagonals.

issues.failure_explanation: For p=1, direct computation from (18) with hat functions at adjacent nodes gives B[l,l] = (d/dt phi_l, d/dt phi_{l-1}) = -1/h and C[l,l] = (d/dt phi_l, phi_{l-1}) = 1/2, so the diagonal of K_h^1(mu) = i B - mu C is -(i/h + mu/2), not -(8i/h + mu/2); the factor 8 is spurious. This is consistent with the paper's own symbol polynomial from Proposition 3.11, q^{B^1}(z) = -1 + 2z - z^2, whose diagonal coefficient (after scaling by h) is -1. The remark's conclusion (invertibility for all h>0 and real mu) remains valid, since -i/h - mu/2 never vanishes for real mu.

failure_location.quote: the system matrix stemming from~\eqref{eq:10} is a lower triangular matrix with entries all equal to~$-\left(8\mi/h +\mu/2\right)$ on the diagonal

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace -(8i/h + mu/2) with -(i/h + mu/2) in the remark.
issues.overall_effect: Only the stated constant in the justification that Assumption 3.4 holds for p=1 is wrong; the conclusion itself (invertibility of the p=1 system matrix) is unaffected.
issues.title: Incorrect diagonal entries claimed for the p=1 system matrix
issues.why_classification: A single wrong constant whose correction (requiring routine recomputation, not visible by inspection) leaves the lower-triangularity argument, the p=1 validity of Assumption 3.4, and all downstream results intact.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In particular, from these expressions, both $q^{\B^p}$ and $q^{\bC^p}$ are reciprocal polynomials, and from \eqref{eq:25}, it follows that $q^{\K^p(\rho)}$ is also a reciprocal polynomial for all $\rho \in \R$.
\K_n^p(\rho) := \mi \B_n^p - \rho \bC_n^p
q^{\mathbf{B}^p}(e^{\mi \theta}) = - e^{\mi p \theta}  B_p(\theta), \quad\quad q^{\mathbf{C}^p}(e^{\mi \theta}) = - e^{\mi p \theta}\mi C_p(\theta).

issues.failure_explanation: q^{C^p} is skew-palindromic (anti-reciprocal), as the proof itself displays. A linear combination i*q^{B^p} - rho*q^{C^p} of a palindromic and an anti-palindromic polynomial is generically neither, so the inference 'both are reciprocal, hence so is q^{K^p(rho)}' is invalid, and the claim is false. Counterexample from the paper's own formulas: for p=1, q^{B^1}(z) = -1+2z-z^2 and q^{C^1}(z) = (z^2-1)/2 (both consistent with Proposition 3.11), so q^{K^1(2)}(z) = (1-i) + 2iz - (1+i)z^2 has roots i and 1, and i^{-1} = -i is not a root. What is true, and suffices for the stated consequence, is that q^{B^p} and q^{C^p} have real coefficients, so z^{2p} * conj(q^{K^p(rho)}(1/conj(z))) = -q^{K^p(rho)}(z): the roots are paired under xi <-> 1/conj(xi), which still forces type (ell, 2p-2ell, ell).

failure_location.quote: The symbol polynomial $q^{\mathbf{K}^p(\rho)}$ of the family $\{ \K_n^p(\rho) \}_n$ defined in \eqref{eq:21} is a reciprocal polynomial.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the reciprocity claim by the conjugate-inverse symmetry: since q^{B^p} (palindromic) and q^{C^p} (anti-palindromic) have real coefficients, q^{K^p(rho)} satisfies z^{2p} conj(q^K(1/conj z)) = -q^K(z), so its zeros are symmetric with respect to inversion in the unit circle; the type (ell, 2p-2ell, ell) and the proposition's consequence then follow verbatim.
issues.overall_effect: Proposition 3.39's stated mechanism is false and its proof invalid; Theorem 3.13 ('Combining Propositions 3.39 and 3.12') and, through it, Theorem 3.42 inherit the gap, although both conclusions survive once the corrected symmetry argument is supplied.
issues.title: Symbol polynomial q^{K^p(rho)} is not reciprocal; proof of Proposition 3.39 is invalid
issues.why_classification: The proposition's headline property is false as stated and must be replaced by a different symmetry via a new (though short) argument; however, the repair is contained and no downstream result is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For~$\rho>0$ and~$p \in \mathbb{N}$, the function $K_p(\theta,\rho)$ has exactly 2 simple zeros
Combining Propositions \ref{prop:39} and \ref{prop:312}, we obtain the main result of the paper.
provided that we show the entries of the two outer codiagonals (the~$k^{\thh}$ and the~$(-m)^{\thh}$) of $\K_n^p(\rho)$ are nonzero for all $\rho>0$ and $p \in \N$

issues.failure_explanation: The entire proof chain (Proposition 3.12 on the zeros of K_p and the outer-codiagonal verification for Theorem 3.9) is carried out only under the hypothesis rho > 0; no argument for rho <= 0 appears anywhere, yet the theorem claims all rho in R (and the section introduction claims all mu in R). Since rho = mu*h and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues mu can be negative (e.g. the potential V = -omega^2 x^2/2 used in Section 5 gives negative mu), the negative-rho half of the claimed range is not covered. The claim is nevertheless true: K_p(-theta,rho) = K_p(theta,-rho) (B_p even, C_p odd, evident from the series in Proposition 3.11) gives rho < 0 by reflection, and for rho = 0, q^{K^p(0)} = i q^{B^p} has a double unit-modulus zero at z = 1 (B_p < 0 on (0,pi]), still giving type (p-1,2,p-1) as required by Theorem 3.8(b), which does not require simple zeros.

failure_location.quote: Then, for all~$p \in \N$ and~$\rho \in \R$, the family of matrices~$\{\K_n^p(\rho)\}_n$ defined in~\eqref{eq:21} is weakly well-conditioned. In other words, the variational formulation in \eqref{eq:10} is unconditionally stable.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the one-line reflection argument for rho < 0 and the degenerate case rho = 0 (double zero at z = 1 counting as two unit-modulus zeros, type (p-1,2,p-1)).
issues.overall_effect: The main theorem's stated parameter range (all rho in R, i.e. unconditional stability for all real mu, including negative eigenvalues) is not established as written for rho <= 0. Theorem 3.42 is unaffected since it only uses the rho > 0 part (mu_s = sqrt(mu_w) > 0).
issues.title: Theorem 3.13 claimed for all real rho but proved only for rho > 0
issues.why_classification: Short, routine additions built from in-source facts; the theorem's statement, method and all conclusions survive intact.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We therefore make the following fundamental assumption in the rest of this section.
Let Assumption \ref{assu:34} be satisfied.
Assume that, for all $p \in \N$ with $p \ge 1$, $h>0$, and $\mu_w > 0$ the variational formulation~\eqref{eq:30} admits a unique solution.

issues.failure_explanation: Assumption 3.4 is explicitly scoped to 'the rest of this section' (Section 3), and Theorem 3.13's conclusion is conditional on it. Theorem 3.42 (Section 4) lists only uniqueness of (30) as hypothesis, yet its proof applies Theorem 3.13 to deduce stability of (10)/(32) for all mu_s in R, i.e. uses Theorem 3.13 outside its hypotheses without establishing Assumption 3.4 in Section 4. The needed implication is true but absent: by the Schur complements already computed in the proof, det M(mu_s) = det(B) det(B + mu_s^2 C B^{-1} C) = det M'(mu_s^2) for mu_s != 0 and M(0) = diag(B,B) with B invertible, so the stated hypothesis does imply Assumption 3.4; the paper never makes this (or any equivalent) argument.

failure_location.quote: Theorem \ref{th:313} guarantees the stability of the variational formulation~\eqref{eq:10}, and, consequently, that of~\eqref{eq:32}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the Schur-determinant argument showing that the theorem's hypothesis (plus the cited invertibility of B) implies Assumption 3.4, or else add Assumption 3.4 explicitly to the hypotheses of Theorem 3.42.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of the paper's second headline result rests on an unstated, out-of-scope hypothesis; the statement of Theorem 3.42 itself is fine once the short derivation is supplied.
issues.title: Proof of Theorem 3.42 invokes Theorem 3.13 without Assumption 3.4 being in force or derived
issues.why_classification: A contained derivation from quantities already present in the proof repairs the dependency; the theorem's statement and conclusion are unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \kappa (\bS)  \le \left(1 + \frac{\| \bC \|^2}{\| \B\|^2} \kappa(\B)\right) \kappa(\bM).
By choosing~$\mu_s = \sqrt{\mu_w}$, the Schur complements for both matrices in~\eqref{eq:33} coincide.

issues.failure_explanation: Lemma A.1 bounds the condition number of the Schur complement S by that of the full matrix M (the M -> S direction). The proof of Theorem 3.42 establishes weak well-conditioning of the Schur complements S' of the (30) matrices M' and then simply asserts that this implies stability of (30), i.e. weak well-conditioning of the system matrices M' themselves. As stated this inference is a non sequitur: conditioning of a Schur complement does not control the conditioning of the full block matrix without additional estimates. The implication is true here, but it requires the block LU factorization M' = L diag(B, S') U with polynomial bounds on kappa(L) and kappa(U) (using ||C|| <= C(p), algebraic kappa(B), and ||B|| >= c/h from the entries of B), none of which is given.

failure_location.quote: Hence, the weakly well-conditioning of these Schur complements implies the stability of formulation~\eqref{eq:30} for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Insert the block-factorization argument: M' = [[I,0],[-mu_w C B^{-1},I]] diag(B,S') [[I, B^{-1}C],[0,I]] with norm bounds yielding kappa(M') <= poly(n) max(kappa(B), kappa(S')).
issues.overall_effect: The concluding step of the proof of the advertised alternative stability proof for the wave-equation method of [FFLP2024] is unsupported as written.
issues.title: Unjustified final step of Theorem 3.42: Schur-complement conditioning does not imply full-matrix conditioning
issues.why_classification: A necessary, contained but genuinely missing matrix-analysis argument must be supplied to repair the proof; the theorem's statement and conclusion survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: (\mi \B_{h_t}^p \otimes \M_{h_{\bx}} + \bC_{h_t}^p \otimes \A_{h_{\bx}}) \boldsymbol{\Psi}^p_{\bh} = \mathbf{F}_{\bh}^p
(\mathbf{Q}_{h_t}^p)^H (\mi \B_{h_t}^p)^{-1} \bC_{h_t}^p \mathbf{Q}_{h_t}^p = \mathbf{R}_{h_t}^p

issues.failure_explanation: Writing S = (iB)^{-1}C = Q R Q^H (step 1), the system matrix of (35) factors as (iB x I)(I x M + Q R Q^H x A); after steps 2-3 the correct reduced system is (R x A + I x M) Z~ = -i (Q^H B^{-1} x I) F with Psi = (Q x I) Z~. The printed step 4 instead uses (R x A + R^{-1} x M), which would require R^{-1} = I (i.e. R = I, false in general; e.g. for p=1 the diagonal of (iB)^{-1}C is i h/2), and the phase in steps 3/5 is correspondingly wrong (even with the M-block corrected, the printed steps return -i times the solution). Hence the algorithm as written solves a different linear system than (35). It can even break down: in the scalar reduction (B = C = M = A = [1]) the step-4 matrix is R x A + R^{-1} x M = -i + i = 0, singular, while the true system i + 1 is nonsingular.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the step-4 matrix by R^p_{h_t} x A_{h_x} + I x M_{h_x} (making the computation of R^{-1} unnecessary) and fix the phase, e.g. step 3 becomes Y <- -i (Q^H x I) Y with step 5 Psi = (Q x I) Z (equivalently, keep step 3 and set Psi = -i (Q x I) Z).
issues.overall_effect: The stated solver does not compute the solution of (35); an implementation following the pseudocode produces wrong (or undefined) output. The structural/efficiency claims (block upper triangular solve, matrix-vector products) remain valid for the corrected version.
issues.title: Algorithm 1 uses the wrong matrix in its main solve step and does not solve system (35)
issues.why_classification: The printed construction provably fails its input-output contract and must be rederived (the wrong R^{-1} x M block and phase are not a single visible slip); the repair is nevertheless local and preserves the method's structure and cost.
